rubric._about: Placeholder written by an onboarding reset. It is not a ladder for any field. Round 2 replaces it with a researched rubric (onboard.rubric); the earlier rubric is archived in prior.json.

levels.1: Starting: does the work with guidance
levels.3: Strong: does it well and teaches others
levels.4: Leading: sets the standard for others

competencies.name: Core skill of your target role

levels.1: Does the core work with guidance
levels.3: Does the core work well and raises the bar for others
levels.4: Sets the standard for the core work

skills._about: Current level per competency (see rubric.json). confidence 0-1 is how sure we are of the level, driven by source quality. history is append-only; every change needs a date, source and reason. target is the next-jump level (senior = 3) unless an active bet sets a nearer one.

core_skill.note: Not assessed yet. Round 2 rates this from evidence.

history.reason: Placeholder written by an onboarding reset. Not assessed yet.

evidence._about: Append-only log of things that happened: work shipped, feedback received, applications, wins, rejections. Each entry has a source type from rubric.json sources. Ratings and proof items point at these ids.

proof._about: Can others SEE that the person can do the work? Each item is an artifact that exists or doesn't. status: missing | draft | done | verified (verified = an outside person has seen and responded to it).

reach._about: Does the market respond? Funnel per application batch, and recognition counters. Only market-source facts go here.

bets._about: A bet = hypothesis + action + metric + target + result. One active bet per track. This is the proof a step was the right one.

week._about: Each day Mon to Sat has one Skill task and one Reach task, about 30 minutes each: tonight's hour. Either can be done first. Sunday is the weekly review. Practice is on new real work. Every task is worth 20 points; points are a simple count of work done, not a grade. Trust comes from the evidence source, not the points.

notnow._about: Things you're deliberately not doing, with the reason. Reviewed every 4 weeks. When the late-night question is 'should I learn X?', check here first.

queue._about: Requests from the app to Claude. The growth-coach skill processes pending items when the person says 'run my queue' in Claude Code, writes results into learning.json / tests.json / skills.json / evidence.json / week.json, and marks them done. type: research | critique | test | plan.

learning._about: Research briefs written by Claude: what experts in the field know at your level, with sources. Each brief is followed by a practice task that applies it.

tests._about: Skill tests. Claude writes the test (scenario questions at the competency's next level) with status 'ready'; you answer in the app ('answered'); Claude scores it ('scored') and the score becomes evidence on the competency.

library._about: Links and resources, each tied to a skill, proof item or bet so nothing is lost in chat.

rubric._about: Product design competencies by level. Levels: 1 junior, 2 mid, 3 senior, 4 lead/staff. Based on public design career ladders (Dropbox, Buffer, Monzo via progression.fyi). The scale is fixed; ratings in skills.json refer to it.

levels.1: Junior: executes defined tasks with guidance
levels.2: Mid: owns features end to end, needs little guidance
levels.3: Senior: owns problem framing and outcomes, raises the bar for others
levels.4: Lead / Staff: sets direction across products or teams, influences strategy, grows designers

levels.2: Frames the user problem before designing; understands the business model of the feature
levels.3: Chooses which problems are worth solving; ties design decisions to metrics and business outcomes
levels.4: Shapes product strategy; defines what the product should become over years

levels.1: Clean screens with help on hierarchy and detail
levels.2: Consistent, polished UI; designs every state of a flow
levels.3: Distinctive, reference-quality work; sets craft standards others follow
levels.4: Defines the visual and interaction language of a product line

levels.2: Builds and documents a system for one product; structures information clearly
levels.3: Runs a system across products and contributors; governs change
levels.4: Designs systems that other teams adopt; sets organisation-wide standards

levels.1: Participates in research run by others
levels.2: Runs lightweight interviews and usability tests; turns findings into design changes
levels.3: Plans research for a product area; combines qualitative and quantitative evidence
levels.4: Builds the team's research practice and evidence culture

levels.2: Presents rationale, handles feedback, writes clear documentation
levels.3: Persuades leadership; tells the story of the work in case studies and talks; gives useful critique
levels.4: Represents design to the company and the industry; shapes how others think

levels.2: Works directly with PM and engineering; takes critique well
levels.3: Mentors other designers; runs critique; unblocks cross-functional teams
levels.4: Hires, grows and leads designers; sets team process

levels.3: Ships working front-end prototypes; uses AI tools to go from design to code
levels.4: Defines how the team designs and builds with AI; ships production-quality front ends

levels.2: Understands the core concepts users face
levels.3: Understands the mechanics well enough to stop misleading UI and challenge engineers and finance
levels.4: Recognised domain expert; others seek their judgement

sources._about: Trust order for any rating or claim. Higher wins when sources disagree.
sources.market: A real market result: screen, interview, offer, inbound message, published feature
sources.expert: A senior designer or hiring manager who reviewed the actual work
sources.shipped: Work that exists and can be inspected: a live product, a document, a repo
